primary_source.title: An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents
primary_source.publication: IEEE Computer, Vol. 26, No. 7, July 1993, pp. 18-41
primary_source.page_mapping: PDF p.01 = printed p.18 ... PDF p.24 = printed p.41. Citations below use 'PDF p.NN / printed p.PP'.
primary_source.why_authoritative: Definitive academic investigation by the foremost software safety researchers, compiled from FDA documents, internal memos, lawsuit depositions and letters; reviewed pre-publication by Ed Miller (FDA) and Gordon Symonds (Canadian Health Protection Branch) [PDF p.24 / printed p.41]

timeline_events.event: Therac-6 software development begins; Therac-25 software later 'evolved' from it
timeline_events.page_or_section: PDF p.03 / printed p.20 (software development sidebar)

timeline_events.event: AECL produces first hardwired Therac-25 prototype; per AECL letter to FDA, 'program structure and certain subroutines were carried over to the Therac 25 around 1976'
Completely computerized commercial Therac-25 available in late 1982; eleven units eventually installed (5 US, 6 Canada)
AECL performs safety analysis (fault tree) that apparently excluded software; assigned 10^-11 to 'Computer selects wrong energy' and 4x10^-9 to 'Computer selects wrong mode' with no justification

Kennestone Regional Oncology Center, Marietta GA: 61-year-old patient overdosed during 10-MeV electron follow-up treatment to lymph nodes near the clavicle after lumpectomy (patient identified in secondary sources as Katherine Yarbrough)

Later in June, Kennestone physicist Tim Still calls AECL asking if the Therac-25 can operate in electron mode without scanning; three days later AECL engineers reply that 'improper scanning was not possible'; no investigation occurs

Ontario Cancer Foundation clinic, Hamilton: 40-year-old patient overdosed on her 24th Therac-25 treatment (cervical carcinoma); machine shut down after ~5 seconds with 'H-tilt', dosimetry read 'no dose', treatment pause; operator proceeded 4 more times (patient identified only in OEC timeline as Frances Hill)

Hamilton patient hospitalized for suspected radiation overexposure; machine taken out of service; AECL sends service engineer; FDA, CRPB and users informed (users say they were not told a patient injury was involved)

AECL letter advises the four US users to visually check the ionization chamber position before treatment and discontinue treatment on an H-tilt message with incorrect dose; letter does not mention a patient injury; FDA terms the Hamilton voluntary recall Class II

AECL microswitch/plunger fixes for the assumed Hamilton cause; AECL letter (dated 16-Sep-85) claims hazard improvement of 'at least five orders of magnitude'; independent consultant for Hamilton clinic recommends a turntable potentiometer in a September 1985 report
timeline_events.page_or_section: PDF p.05, p.09, p.10 / printed p.22, 26, 27

timeline_events.event: Kennestone patient files suit against AECL and the hospital. Paper's own accounts conflict: event timeline says October; main text says 'filed on November 13, 1985'; Tim Still (via Tyler physicist) says filed October 1985 with AECL officially notified in November 1985

Hamilton patient dies of an extremely virulent cancer; autopsy gives cancer as cause of death but notes a total hip replacement would have been required due to the radiation overexposure; AECL technician later estimates 13,000-17,000 rads delivered
CRPB (Canada) letter to AECL asking for additional hardware interlocks and software changes
timeline_events.page_or_section: PDF p.05 / printed p.22 (event timeline); PDF p.09 / printed p.26

timeline_events.event: Yakima Valley Memorial Hospital, WA: woman develops parallel striped erythema on right hip after Therac-25 treatment; cause not recognized as abnormal until Jan-Feb 1986; her treatments completed Jan 6, 1986
Yakima staff letter to AECL reporting overdose possibility (plus phone call to AECL technical support supervisor)

AECL technical support supervisor's written reply: damage 'could not have been produced by any malfunction of the Therac-25 or by any operator error', with two pages of reasons and the claim of 'apparently no other instances of similar damage' (Kennestone and Hamilton had already occurred)

East Texas Cancer Center, Tyler TX: male patient on 9th treatment overdosed twice (Malfunction 54 both times); est. 16,500-25,000 rads in under 1 second over ~1 cm2 (patient identified in 1986 press and secondary sources as Voyne Ray Cox)

Therac-25 shut down for testing; local AECL engineer plus one from the home office cannot reproduce Malfunction 54; home-office engineer says overdose is not possible; AECL says it knows of no other overexposure accidents and suggests an electrical problem (engineers named Randy Rhodes and Dave Nott in OEC timeline only)
Tyler machine put back into service after independent engineering firm finds no electrical grounding problem

Second Tyler overdose: same operator, same cursor-up edit; Malfunction 54; patient receiving electron treatment for facial skin cancer (identified in 1986-87 press and secondary sources as Verdon Kidd); physicist Fritz Hager and the operator reproduce the fault, establishing data-entry speed as the key factor
AECL files accident report with FDA and sends users the cursor-up letter: remove the UP key cap and fix the contacts open with electrical tape; FDA later rejects the letter as inadequate notification
Second Tyler patient dies three weeks after the accident; autopsy shows acute high-dose radiation injury to the right temporal lobe and brain stem
FDA declares the Therac-25 defective under the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act; demands a corrective action plan (CAP) and proper renotification of users
AECL submits original six-item CAP to FDA
FDA conceptually agrees with CAP but demands software descriptions, development documentation, revised requirements, interaction analysis and a documented test plan

First Therac-25 user group meeting at the annual AAPM conference; first Tyler patient dies of overdose complications five months after the March 21 accident (secondary sources conflict on exact date: OEC says Aug 1986, Rose 1994 says Sept 20, 1986)
AECL sends software documents but no test plan: 'no single test plan and report exists for the software'; claims CAP improves safety 'by many orders of magnitude'

FDA complains about insufficient accident description and flow-diagram detail; internal memo (Oct 20) flags 'apparent paucity of software QA at the manufacturing facility' and AECL's prior knowledge of the Nov 1985 Georgia lawsuit
CAP Revision 1: twelve new software-modification items plus a test plan
Therac-20 users notified of a software bug (the Therac-25 race-condition error had been found in Therac-20 software via Frank Borger's blown-fuse investigation)
FDA requires dosimetry malfunctions to suspend (not pause) treatment, better operator warnings, copying QA and rigorous testing standards for future modifications
CAP Revision 2 submitted (dose malfunctions suspend treatment; highlighted dose error messages; expanded diagrams; hardware+software test plan)

Second Yakima overdose: 65-year-old male patient (identified only in OEC timeline as Glen A. Dodd) receives est. 8,000-10,000 rads over two attempts vs 86 rads prescribed; Class3 byte-overflow bug with turntable in field-light position

AECL sends FDA its Component and Installation Test Plan; AECL calls users with detailed avoidance instructions (nine days after the accident); Ed Miller conference call with AECL QA manager links Hamilton to the Yakima bug
AECL announces to customers: corrected software (Tyler + Yakima bugs), hardware single-pulse shutdown circuit, turntable potentiometer, hardware turntable interlock circuit
Ed Miller (FDA) calls Pavel Dvorak (Health and Welfare Canada): FDA will recommend all Therac-25s be shut down until permanent modifications are made; Dvorak agrees

FDA Notice of Adverse Findings: Therac-25 defective under US law; AECL must notify purchasers and recommend discontinuing routine therapy use until an amended CAP is fully completed; Canada's Health Protection Branch does the same (AECL complies by letters Feb 20); suspension lasts until August 1987

Second user group meeting: AECL, all users with technical and legal staff, FDA, Canadian BRMD, AECB, Province of Ontario, Canadian Association of Physicists committee; participants review all six known major accidents and produce a prioritized modification list
CAP Revision 3 sent to FDA (covers both Tyler and Yakima bugs; four additional software modifications; software turntable position interlock)
timeline_events.page_or_section: PDF p.05 / printed p.22 (event timeline; resolves OCR-uncertain date on PDF p.18)

timeline_events.event: Second Yakima patient dies of complications related to the overdose; he had a pre-existing terminal cancer; survivors' lawsuit settled out of court
FDA finds CAP appendix turntable-interlock signal descriptions reversed (high/low swapped); questions potentiometer reliability and backspace-key edit behavior
CAP Revision 4 incorporating FDA comments and user-group input

FDA approves CAP subject to final test results, independent safety analysis, revised manual and completion by June 30; rates it a Class I recall (reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death)

AECL sends CAP test plan, draft manual and draft safety analysis; the safety analysis reveals four potentially hazardous subsystems not covered by CAP Rev 4 (electron-beam scanning, energy selection, beam shutoff, calibration/steering)
Fifth and final CAP revision sent to FDA (FDA had given verbal approval at the July user group meeting; full implementation expected by end of August 1987)
Interim safety analysis report issued
Final safety analysis report issued; full CAP implementation including the safety analysis took more than two years after the Tyler accidents

AECL Medical begins separation from AECL; division later privatized as Theratronics International Ltd (paper, 1993: 'in the process of being privatized and is now called Theratronics International Limited'); Wikipedia dates the AECL Medical dissolution to 1988
timeline_events.page_or_section: corroborated at PDF p.02 / printed p.19

timeline_events.event: Safety-analysis-driven hardware modifications scheduled for completion around mid-1989, final software updates extending into late 1989 or early 1990 (OCR-uncertain date)
timeline_events.page_or_section: PDF p.19 / printed p.36 (sidebar; OCR garbled)

timeline_events.event: US comptroller general testifies to Congress on incident-reporting viability; GAO study: FDA knows of less than 1 percent of deaths, serious injuries, or equipment malfunctions occurring in hospitals
US law amended to require health-care facilities (not just manufacturers/importers) to report device incidents to manufacturer and FDA
Leveson publishes 'The Therac-25: 30 Years Later' (IEEE Computer 50(11), pp. 8-11): the accidents were 'simply the first of many, as these types of radiation-overdose accidents continue today'

stakeholders.note: Leveson 1993 anonymizes her (case details match PDF p.04-06 / printed p.21-23). Name established by Rose, 'Fatal Dose' (1994 journalism) and OEC timeline; entered public record via her 1985 lawsuit. Rose reports she died 1990 in a traffic accident, unrelated to the overdose.

data_points.claim: Eleven Therac-25s were installed (five in the US, six in Canada); six accidents involving massive overdoses occurred between 1985 and 1987; the machine was recalled in 1987 for extensive design changes including hardware safeguards against software errors
The paper calls the Therac-25 accidents 'the most serious computer-related accidents to date (at least nonmilitary and admitted)'

Leveson's canonical casualty phrasing (2017): the machine 'massively overdosed six people, resulting in serious injury and deaths' -- she never states a specific death count; deaths verified per-case in the 1993 paper: Tyler patient 2 died May 1, 1986; Tyler patient 1 died five months after his accident; Yakima 1987 patient died April 1987 of overdose complications
data_points.page_or_section: 2017 p.8; PDF p.11, p.16 / printed p.28, 33

data_points.claim: The Therac-25 was a dual-mode, double-pass linear accelerator delivering 25-MeV photons or 5-25 MeV electrons; the double-pass design made it notably more compact, more versatile, 'arguably easier to use' and more economic to produce (magnetron rather than klystron); one machine for both modalities was an economic advantage for customers

On the predecessor Therac-6 and Therac-20, 'the computer merely added convenience to the existing hardware, which was capable of standing alone. Industry-standard hardware safety features and interlocks in the underlying machines were retained'

Interlock removal was a corporate AECL design decision, not one attributed to any named individual: 'AECL took advantage of the computer's abilities to control and monitor the hardware and decided not to duplicate all the existing hardware safety mechanisms and interlocks'; the paper frames the motive as an industry trend -- 'companies decide that hardware interlocks and backups are not worth the expense, or they put more faith (perhaps misplaced) on software than on hardware reliability' -- and lists 'overconfidence in the software' as a contributing factor

The Therac-20 had independent protective circuits for monitoring electron-beam scanning plus mechanical interlocks; 'In the Therac-25, software checks were substituted for many traditional hardware interlocks'

The software was developed by a single person in PDP-11 assembly language over several years; it 'evolved' from Therac-6 software begun in 1972, with 'program structure and certain subroutines carried over to the Therac 25 around 1976' -- the code lineage predates the commercial machine by a decade
data_points.page_or_section: PDF p.03 / printed p.20 (software development sidebar)

data_points.claim: The programmer left AECL in 1986; in lawsuit depositions no AECL employee could provide any information about his educational background or experience, and the suit settled before he could be deposed: 'We have been unable to learn anything about his background'. His software ran as a custom stand-alone real-time executive (not a standard OS) on a 32K PDP 11/23, with a preemptive scheduler initiating tasks every 0.1 second

Root design flaw: 'the software allowed concurrent access to shared memory... there is no real synchronization aside from data stored in shared variables, and... the test and set for such variables are not indivisible operations. Race conditions resulting from this implementation of multitasking played an important part in the accidents'

AECL's March 1983 fault-tree safety analysis apparently excluded software, assuming programming errors had been 'reduced by extensive testing' and that software does not degrade; it assigned 10^-11 to 'Computer selects wrong energy' and 4x10^-9 to 'Computer selects wrong mode' -- 'The report provides no justification of either number'

Software testing was minimal: AECL's QA manager said the Therac-25 software was tested for 2,700 hours, clarified under user questioning as '2,700 hours of use'; a 'small amount' of testing on a simulator, most as integrated system; later, AECL admitted 'no single test plan and report exists for the software'; an FDA reviewer on the final CAP test data: 'Amazingly, the test data presented to show that the software changes... are appropriate prove the exact opposite result... Where is the QC review for the test program?'
data_points.page_or_section: PDF p.03, p.15, p.20 / printed p.20, 32, 37

data_points.claim: Dual-mode physics of the hazard: a rotating turntable moves accessories into the beam path for three cardinal positions (electron mode, X-ray mode, field light -- the last with a stainless steel mirror, no ion chamber, no beam expected), monitored by three microswitches as a 3-bit signal; X-ray mode requires electron-beam current ~100 times higher than electron therapy because the 'beam flattener' (an inverted-ice-cream-cone attenuator) eats most of the output; 'If the machine produces a photon beam with the beam flattener not in position, a high output dose rate results. This is the basic hazard of dual-mode machines: If the turntable is in the wrong position, the beam flattener will not be in place'

Usability-over-safety interface history: operators complained initial data entry took too long, so the manufacturer modified the software to let carriage returns copy treatment-site data -- 'This interface modification was to figure in several accidents'
data_points.page_or_section: PDF p.07 / printed p.24 (operator interface sidebar)

data_points.claim: Treatment pause vs suspend: a 'treatment pause' (low priority) required only the single-key 'P' to proceed, retaining all treatment parameters; it could be invoked up to five times before automatic suspend; a suspend required a full machine reset

Error messages were cryptic -- some just 'malfunction' plus a number 1-64 denoting an analog/digital channel; per an FDA memorandum, the operator's manual did not explain or even address the malfunction codes and the materials gave 'no indication that these malfunctions could place a patient at risk'

Operator habituation (sworn testimony): an operator involved in an overdose 'had become insensitive to machine malfunctions'; malfunction messages were commonplace -- 'It was not out of the ordinary for something to stop the machine... I can't remember all the reasons it would stop, but there were a lot of them'; she had been taught there were 'so many safety mechanisms' that overdose was 'virtually impossible'; a radiation therapist at another clinic reported an average of 40 dose-rate malfunctions, attributed to underdoses, on some days

Kennestone, June 3, 1985: a 61-year-old patient receiving follow-up treatment after lumpectomy (10-MeV electron treatment to lymph nodes near the clavicle) was overdosed; the Therac-25 had been at Kennestone about six months; other units had operated 'apparently without incident' since 1983

Kennestone patient's documented account: she felt a 'tremendous force of heat... this red-hot sensation' and told the technician 'You burned me'; the technician replied 'that was not possible'; there were no visible marks at the time though the treatment area felt 'warm to the touch'

Kennestone display/indication: the paper records no malfunction message or overdose indication for this accident; details are 'sketchy since it was never carefully investigated'; the treatment prescription printout feature was disabled at the time, so no hard copy of treatment data existed. (The often-scripted line that readouts 'indicated a normal treatment' is from the OEC educational timeline, not the primary paper; no verbatim screen text exists in any source.)
data_points.source_name: Leveson & Turner 1993 (display detail); OEC timeline (normal-readout phrasing)

data_points.claim: Kennestone dose: the physicist later estimated one or two doses in the 15,000-20,000 rad range and believed the injury required at least 8,000 rads; typical single therapeutic doses are ~200 rads; 500 rads whole-body is the accepted 50%-lethality figure

Kennestone outcome: the patient survived; the radiation injury eventually required removal of her breast; she completely lost the use of her shoulder and arm and was in constant pain; her lawsuit settled out of court. (Secondary source Rose 1994: she died in 1990 in a traffic accident, unrelated to the overdose.)

AECL's response to Kennestone was a phone assertion, not an investigation: physicist Tim Still called AECL asking whether an unscanned electron-mode beam was possible; three days later AECL engineers called back to say 'improper scanning was not possible'; the paper states 'no investigation occurred at this time' and FDA investigators later cited AECL's lack of any mechanism to follow up reports of suspected accidents

Regulatory blind spot: the Kennestone accident was not reported to the FDA until after the 1986 Tyler accidents -- reporting regulations then bound only manufacturers and importers, not users; the law was amended in 1990 to require health-care facilities to report; a GAO study (1989 congressional testimony) found the FDA knows of less than 1 percent of deaths, serious injuries, or device malfunctions occurring in hospitals

Hamilton, July 26, 1985: 40-year-old patient, 24th Therac-25 treatment; machine shut down after ~5 seconds with 'H-tilt', dosimetry display read 'no dose', status 'treatment pause'; following standard procedure the operator pressed 'P' and repeated four more times, the display showing 'no dose' each time; after the fifth pause the machine suspended; the called-in technician found nothing wrong -- also 'not unusual'

Hamilton outcome: patient hospitalized July 30, 1985; died November 3, 1985 of an extremely virulent cancer -- autopsy attributed death to the cancer but noted a total hip replacement would have been required because of the radiation overexposure; an AECL technician estimated 13,000-17,000 rads delivered

Hamilton diagnosis collapse: AECL could not reproduce the malfunction, assumed a transient microswitch failure 'even though the engineers were unable to reproduce the failure or find anything wrong with the microswitch', and its final report said it 'cannot be firm on the exact cause'; AECL's September 1985 letter claimed the fix improved safety 'by at least five orders of magnitude' -- a claim the paper calls 'hard to justify'; the FDA's Miller later recorded that the Hamilton accident probably had the same cause as the 1987 Yakima overflow bug and that 'the subsequent recall of the multiple microswitch logic network did not really solve the problem'
data_points.page_or_section: PDF p.09, p.16, p.22 / printed p.26, 33, 39

data_points.claim: The five-orders claim disarmed the next victim's hospital: the Yakima physicist wrote that because AECL's letter claimed 'an improvement of at least five orders of magnitude' (which the staff read as 10,000,000 percent), 'we did not believe that there could have been any accelerator malfunction' when their own patient was injured in December 1985

Ignored independent recommendations: a consultant's September 1985 report for the Hamilton clinic recommended an independent turntable-position potentiometer; the CRPB wrote AECL in November 1985 requesting additional hardware interlocks and software changes; the Hamilton clinic's attorney wrote in January 1986 citing continuing turntable problems including four incidents at Hamilton -- 'AECL did not comply: No independent interlock was installed on the Therac-25s at this time'

Yakima December 1985: striped erythema matched the slots of the beam-blocking trays, but the trays had been discarded before the reaction was recognized as abnormal; staff even X-rayed the patient's heating pad to test an alternative explanation -- the wire pattern did not correspond; outcome: chronic skin ulcer and subdermal tissue necrosis, surgically repaired with grafts; patient alive in 1993 with minor disability and scarring

AECL's written reply to Yakima (Feb 24, 1986): the damage 'could not have been produced by any malfunction of the Therac-25 or by any operator error', supported by two pages of technical reasons plus the claim of 'apparently no other instances of similar damage' -- although the Kennestone and Hamilton accidents had occurred and AECL had received lawsuit notification in November 1985

Tyler context, March 21, 1986: the Therac-25 had treated more than 500 patients over two years at ETCC; the patient was on his ninth treatment (180 rads of a 6,000-rad/6.5-week prescription, 22-MeV electron mode); the operator was experienced and fast, and typing 'x' (X-ray) instead of 'e' (electron) was a common mistake she fixed with the cursor-up key

Malfunction 54 meaning: the sheet on the side of the machine said it was a 'dose input 2' error; an AECL technician testified this meant a dose had been delivered 'either too high or too low'; ETCC had no other documentation explaining it; the machine displayed it with a low-priority 'treatment pause'

Tyler display deception: after a massive overdose the dose monitor showed a substantial UNDERDOSE -- 6 monitor units delivered vs 202 requested; accustomed to frequent harmless stops, the operator took the normal action and pressed 'P'; the machine delivered a second overdose with the same 'Malfunction 54' and the same underdose reading

On the day of the first Tyler accident the operator was isolated: the video display to the shielded treatment room was unplugged and the audio monitor was broken; the patient -- who knew from eight prior sessions this was abnormal -- reported sensations like electric shock and 'hot coffee' poured on his back, was getting off the table when the second dose was triggered, and pounded on the treatment room door

Tyler dose: after-the-fact simulations indicated possible doses of 16,500-25,000 rads in under 1 second over an area of about 1 cm2; clinical course: radiation-induced myelitis of the cervical cord, paralysis of the left arm, both legs, left vocal cord and left diaphragm; death from overdose complications five months after the accident

AECL response to Tyler 1: engineers could not reproduce Malfunction 54; the home-office engineer said it was 'not possible for the Therac-25 to overdose a patient'; AECL personnel told the ETCC physicist they knew of no other overexposure accidents -- which the paper calls odd given Hamilton (7 months earlier), Yakima, and the Georgia lawsuit; AECL suggested an electrical problem; an independent firm found no grounding fault and the machine returned to service April 7, 1986. (An AECL QC manager also testified that 'cursor up' problems had been found at Kennestone and another clinic in early and mid 1985 and were twice thought fixed.)

Tyler 2, April 11, 1986: same operator, same cursor-up mode edit; the machine shut down with a loud noise audible through the now-working intercom, displaying Malfunction 54; the patient reported 'fire' on the side of his face, a flash of light, and a sound like frying eggs; he died May 1, 1986; autopsy showed acute high-dose radiation injury to the right temporal lobe and brain stem

Hager's reproduction: physicist Fritz Hager worked with the operator, who remembered her exact keystrokes; they determined data-entry speed during editing was the key factor; it took practice before Hager could elicit Malfunction 54 at will; his first measurement read ~804 rads but the ion chamber had saturated -- adjusted, he determined the dose was over 4,000 rads; AECL could not reproduce the fault until told to perform the procedure rapidly, then measured 25,000 rads at field center; an AECL engineer explained the frying sound as the ion chambers saturating

Therac-20 blown fuses (the proof that removal killed): at the University of Chicago's teaching clinic, fuses and breakers tripped whenever a new student class started -- physicist Frank Borger traced 'creative methods of editing' to the SAME computer bug as the Therac-25; on the Therac-20 the error was 'just a nuisance' because independent hardware protective circuits 'do not allow the beam to turn on, so there is no danger of radiation exposure to a patient'; Borger notified the FDA, which notified Therac-20 users (December 1986)
data_points.page_or_section: PDF p.12 / printed p.29; summary at PDF p.04, p.22 / printed p.21, 39

data_points.claim: Race-condition mechanics: mode/energy lives in the 2-byte shared variable MEOS -- one byte drives the turntable task (Hand), the other indexes operating parameters (Datent); 'The software appears to include no checks to detect such an incompatibility'; setting the bending magnets takes ~8 seconds, and the Ptime delay subroutine clears the 'editing taking place' flag on its first pass -- so an edit completed within the 8-second magnet-setting window updates the screen but not the machine; a second, residual race condition (cursor-position flag) required AECL's later fix

Yakima 1987 bug -- Class3 byte overflow: the Set-Up Test subroutine incremented the 1-byte shared variable Class3 on every pass (several hundred passes per setup); on every 256th pass it rolled over to zero, and the upper-collimator check (Chkcol) was silently skipped; 'The overexposure occurred when the operator hit the set button at the precise moment that Class3 rolled over to zero... The software turned on the full 25 MeV without the target in place and without scanning'; AECL's fix was described as 'simple' -- set Class3 to a fixed nonzero value instead of incrementing

Yakima 1987 accident and display: prescription totaled 86 rads (4 + 3 rad film exposures + 79-rad photon treatment); console showed 'beam ready', operator keyed 'B'; the beam came on but NO dose or dose rate displayed; after 5-6 seconds the unit paused with a message that 'may have disappeared quickly'; the operator pressed 'P'; second pause showed 'FLATNESS'; afterward the console displayed only the 7 rads of the film exposures -- AECL measurements put the actual delivery at 4,000-5,000 rads per attempt, 8,000-10,000 rads over the two attempts

Yakima 1987 investigation: all AECL tests 'indicated that the machine was working perfectly'; 'The investigators could not reproduce the fault condition that produced the 1987 Yakima overdose'; after a week of hardware checks AECL concluded the behavior 'was probably not caused by hardware alone' and then found the software flaw; an AECL QA manager said the Tyler retrofits -- scheduled nine months earlier but not yet installed -- would have prevented the accident

The FDA learned of the Tyler accidents from the Texas state health department, not from AECL; the Therac-25 had reached market through pre-market notification (substantial equivalence), not pre-market approval -- the FDA was 'basically reactive to problems'

AECL's first 'fix' (letter of April 15, 1986, complete text in paper): the cursor UP key 'must not be used for editing or any other purpose'; 'the key cap must be removed and the switch contacts fixed in the open position with electrical tape or other insulating material'; the FDA compliance director rejected it: it 'does not describe the defect nor the hazards' and 'implies the inconvenience to operators outweighs the need to disable the key' (naming AECL's Mr. Downs)

CAP saga: FDA declared the Therac-25 defective under the Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act on May 2, 1986, ordering AECL to notify all purchasers, investigate, determine a solution and submit a corrective action plan; original six-item CAP June 13, 1986; FDA pushback July 23, Oct 30, Dec 11, 1986 and Apr 9, 1987; Revisions Nov 12, 1986; Dec 22, 1986; Mar 5, 1987; May 1, 1987; and the fifth/final July 21, 1987; conditional FDA approval May 26, 1987 with Class I recall rating; the final CAP comprised more than 20 hardware/software changes plus documentation; full implementation including the safety analysis took more than two years after the Tyler accidents (final safety analysis report Nov 3, 1988)

FDA shutdown, February 1987: Ed Miller told Canada (Pavel Dvorak) on Feb 6 the FDA would recommend all Therac-25s out of service until permanent modifications; the Feb 10 Notice of Adverse Findings required AECL to notify purchasers and recommend discontinuing routine therapy 'until such time that an amended corrective action plan approved by CDRH is fully completed'; Canada's Health Protection Branch acted in parallel; the suspension lasted until August 1987

FDA internal memo (Feb 18, 1987): 'It is impossible for CDRH to find all potential failure modes and conditions of the software... I am not convinced that there are not other software glitches that could result in serious injury'; the same memo cites a Jan 21, 1987 AECL bulletin admitting that edit keys pressed after the 'B' (beam on) command were interpreted as a carriage return and INITIATED EXPOSURE, and that doses below a preset value silently defaulted to a 'phantom table' value unbeknownst to the operator

March 1987 joint meeting (regulators, all users, AECL): participants reviewed 'all the six known major Therac-25 accidents'; the AECL QA manager said CAP tests had been done but 'were not documented', that independent software evaluation 'might not be possible', could not name the two outside experts said to have reviewed the software, said memory limits ruled out an audit-trail option, and refused to release source code to users

User group findings (1986): an interlock checking gun current, added by the Vancouver clinic to its own machine, was labeled 'redundant' by AECL -- users disagreed; design problems caused 10-30 percent underdosing in both modes; Tim Still's newsletter letter listed eight major problems and asked 'Is programming safety relying too much on the software interlock routines?'

Final CAP safety features: all dosimetry interruptions go to suspend; software AND independent hardware single-pulse shutdown circuits; turntable potentiometer giving operators a visible position signal; interlocking with the 270-degree bending magnet so target and flattener must be in place in X-ray mode; beam-on prevented in field-light or intermediate turntable positions; meaningful error messages; editing keys limited; a motion-enable 'dead man's' footswitch; plus 23 other software changes -- hardware interlocks were reinstated

AECL's own final safety analysis (FMEA/fault tree/code inspection) treated all software faults as a single event, used a generic software failure rate justified 'based on the historical performance of the Therac-25 software', and its outside code inspection declared beam shutoff, symmetry control and dose calibration code 'straightforward' with 'no execution path' to incorrect behavior -- while conceding inspection 'was unable to provide a high level of confidence' for scanning and energy selection, which therefore got hardware interlocks; Leveson: 'it is difficult to understand how any part of the code could be labeled straightforward'

The machine could not tell the truth about overdoses: 'The Therac-25 software lied to the operators, and the machine itself could not detect that a massive overdose had occurred. The Therac-25 ion chambers could not handle the high density of ionization from the unscanned electron beam at high-beam current; they thus became saturated and gave an indication of a low dosage'; 'Patient reactions were the only real indications of the seriousness of the problems'

'The Therac-20 contained the same software error implicated in the Tyler deaths, but the machine included hardware interlocks that mitigated its consequences'; stated lesson: 'not to remove standard hardware interlocks when adding computer control'

'There is always another software bug': the paper warns against believing a cause was found without adequate evidence (the Hamilton microswitch) and against assuming that fixing one error prevents future accidents; 'Fixing each individual software flaw as it was found did not solve the device's safety problems'; 'Accidents are seldom simple -- they usually involve a complex web of interacting events with multiple contributing technical, human, and organizational factors'

Reuse lesson (1993 and 2017): 'Reusing software modules does not guarantee safety in the new system... Safety is a quality of the system in which the software is used; it is not a quality of the software itself' (1993); 'Reusing software that was safe in one system doesn't mean it will be safe when used in a different system' (2017)

'It was users who found the problems with the Therac-25 and forced AECL to respond. The process of fixing the Therac-25 was user driven -- the manufacturer was slow to respond'; once involved, the FDA's response 'was impressive, especially considering how little experience they had with similar problems in computerized medical devices'

Miller (FDA, 1987) on why testing cannot save you: the accidents required 'operator action within very narrow time-frame windows'; 'It is unlikely that software testing will discover all possible errors... These machines, for example, have been exercised for thousands of hours in the factory and in the hospitals without accident'; 'I, for one, will not be surprised if other software errors appear with this or other equipment in the future'

Canada's CRPB demanded after Hamilton -- months before Tyler -- that a malfunction terminate treatment without a single-keystroke proceed option (letter of Nov 8, 1985 under the Radiation Emitting Devices Act, per OEC; the primary paper confirms a Nov 1985 CRPB letter requesting additional hardware interlocks and software changes and that AECL did not comply)

unverifiable_claims: Patient names: the primary paper anonymizes all six patients. Yarbrough, Cox and Kidd are corroborated by 1986-94 journalism (Boston Globe 6/20/1986, NY Times 6/21/1986, Joyce/American Medical News, Rose 'Fatal Dose' 1994); 'Frances Hill' and 'Glen A. Dodd' trace ONLY to the Online Ethics Center timeline (single curated source, not journalism) -- flag any on-screen name card for these two accordingly. The December 1985 Yakima patient has no verified name in any source.

PSEUDONYM TRAP: ComputingCases.org's Therac-25 teaching narrative (mirrored at bohr.wlu.ca and inside onlineethics.org case materials) uses a fictionalized name set with no disclaimer: Linda Knight (=Yarbrough), Donna Gartner (=Hill), Janis Tilman (=Yakima 1985), Isaac Dahl (=Cox), Daniel McCarthy (=Kidd), Anders Engman (=Dodd). These circulate in course materials and AI summaries; they are NOT real names. ComputingCases also misdates Tyler 1 as March 22 (primary: March 21).

CONFLICT - Kennestone lawsuit date: the primary paper itself conflicts (event timeline: October 1985; main text: 'filed on November 13, 1985'; Tim Still via the Tyler physicist: filed October 1985, AECL officially notified November 1985). OEC says Nov 18, 1985; Rose 1994 says October 1985. Use 'autumn 1985' or 'filed in late 1985; AECL formally notified that November'.

CONFLICT - Tyler patient 1 death date: primary says only 'five months after the accident' (= ~late August 1986); OEC timeline says August 1986; Rose 1994 says September 20, 1986 with radiation overdose on the death certificate. Unresolved; prefer 'five months after the accident, in 1986'.

CONFLICT - Tyler patient 2 treatment site: OEC says left ear with autopsy injury to the RIGHT temporal lobe; Rose 1994 and web sources say right ear; the primary says only 'skin cancer on the side of his face' and right-temporal-lobe injury at autopsy. Script should say 'face' without a side.

OEC timeline lists 'Debbie Cox and Cox family file lawsuit -- September 23, 1996', almost certainly a typo for 1986 (the entry sits between Aug 1986 and Sept 26, 1986 rows). Do not cite the 1996 date.

CONFLICT - software origin year: Leveson 2017 says 'The Therac-25 software was created in 1974'; the 1993 paper says the Therac-6 software it evolved from 'was started in 1972' with structure carried over 'around 1976'. Use the 1993 page-cited lineage; if citing 2017, quote it as her later characterization.

'Verdon Kidd was the first person ever killed by a radiation-therapy overdose / by software' -- editorial characterization attributed to Jonathan Jacky ('first fatality from radiation overdose during treatment'); the primary paper never makes a 'first ever' claim. Attribute, do not state as fact.

Script overreach check (seg_024-type lines): 'at every step the manufacturer said the same thing' is contradicted by the record -- documented impossibility denials cover Kennestone (June 1985 callback), Yakima 1 (Feb 24, 1986 letter) and Tyler 1 (March 1986); after Tyler 2 AECL acknowledged a software problem and engaged in the CAP process.

'One of the most widely cited case studies in software engineering' (seg_035-type line): no citation-count source gathered; soften to 'a standard case study, still taught and revisited by its original investigator 30 years later' (groundable via Leveson 2017).

Generic software failure rate in AECL's safety analysis: OCR drops the exponent; 10^-4/hour is the figure published elsewhere but is UNCERTAIN from the local copy (PDF p.19 / printed p.36). Verify against a clean copy before quoting a number.
Mid-1989 completion date for safety-analysis hardware modifications is OCR-garbled in the local copy (PDF p.19 / printed p.36); treat as approximate.
KLTV 2026 detail that AECL's $10M insurance policy paid ~$1M to ETCC with the remainder to injured patients: single 2026 local-news source, uncorroborated; medium confidence at best.
AECL 'stopped selling therapy machines in 1985' (Jacky) conflicts with documented Therac-25 support through 1987-88; likely refers to new-model sales -- avoid using.

Per-source dose spreads to preserve: Kennestone 15,000-20,000 rads (primary, with >=8,000 floor); Hamilton 13,000-17,000 rads (primary AECL estimate; Rose says ~17,000); Tyler 16,500-25,000 rads (primary simulation range); Yakima 1987 8,000-10,000 rads cumulative (primary). The paper itself warns exact doses are unknowable (PDF p.12 / printed p.29).

Modern_relevance below is limited to what the retrospective sweep and primary sources verify; contemporaneous press citations are carried via Jacky's reference list, not independently fetched.

misconceptions: One bug caused all accidents (there were at least two distinct bugs, and the causes of Kennestone/Hamilton/Yakima-1985 were never definitively established -- PDF p.16 / printed p.33)

The programmer was negligent (the paper explicitly rejects single-cause blame; the software was reused from machines with hardware backups, and the programmer's identity/background were never even established)

FDA failed to act (declared defective May 1986, forced 5 CAP revisions, recommended shutdown Feb 1987; the 1993 paper calls its response 'impressive' once involved -- the gap was the reporting regime before involvement)
All the injured patients died (three of six died of overdose complications; Kennestone and Yakima-1985 patients survived with disability; the Hamilton patient died of her cancer)
The machine showed an overdose error (displays showed underdoses, 'no dose', or nothing -- the software 'lied')

modern_relevance.note: The dedicated modern-relevance sweep report was missing at synthesis time; entries below are limited to present-tense facts verified by the retrospective sweep (Leveson 2017, KLTV 2026) and the primary papers. Post-2017 regulatory status and modern incident statistics remain open research gaps.

facts.claim: Leveson (2017): the Therac-25 'wasn't an anomaly but simply the first of many, as these types of radiation-overdose accidents continue today', citing Bogdanich's NYT investigation 'A Pinpoint Beam Strays Invisibly, Harming Instead of Healing' (Dec 28, 2010)
facts.source_name: Leveson, 'The Therac-25: 30 Years Later', IEEE Computer 50(11)

facts.claim: Leveson's 2017 regulatory verdict: the FDA's original response 'was impressive'; 'later follow-through was weak, as is current regulation of medical device software'

Leveson 2017 on risk math: the Therac-25 HAD a probabilistic risk assessment, updated after an early accident, which 'led to dangerous complacency'; re-quoting 1993: 'In our enthusiasm to provide measurements, we should not attempt to measure the unmeasurable'

Leveson 2017 reuse warning, present tense: 'Reusing software that was safe in one system doesn't mean it will be safe when used in a different system. Safety is a quality of the system in which the software is used; it's not a quality of the software itself'

Fritz Hager, interviewed 40 years on (2026): 'I told my administrator -- We've just killed somebody.'; he reproduced the fault after ~3 hours of after-hours experimentation with the operator, with typing speed the key variable; ETCC stopped using the machine immediately

The case remains standard teaching material in software engineering and ethics curricula (OEC case materials maintained; Leveson herself revisited it in IEEE Computer in 2017) -- but teaching versions circulate with fictionalized patient names (see pseudonym trap)

The 1990 US reporting amendment (health-care facilities must report device incidents to manufacturer and FDA) -- the regulatory regime change directly traceable to this case -- remains the foundation of user-facility reporting
